title: 2024 AMC 10B Problem 21
statement: Two straight pipes (circular cylinders), with radii \(1\) and \(\tfrac14,\) lie parallel and in contact on a flat floor. The figure below shows a head-on view. What is the sum of the possible radii of a third parallel pipe lying on the same floor and in contact with both?

solutions.text: Two circles of radii \(R\) and \(r\) resting on the floor and touching each other have contact points a horizontal distance \(2\sqrt{Rr}\) apart. So the radius-\(1\) and radius-\(\tfrac14\) pipes touch the floor \(2\sqrt{1 \cdot \tfrac14} = 1\) apart. A third pipe of radius \(r\) sits \(2\sqrt{r}\) from the big pipe’s contact point and \(2\sqrt{\tfrac14 r} = \sqrt{r}\) from the small pipe’s. Nestled between them, \(2\sqrt r + \sqrt r = 1,\) so \(\sqrt r = \tfrac13\) and \(r = \tfrac19.\) Sitting past the small pipe, \(2\sqrt r - \sqrt r = 1,\) so \(r = 1.\) (Past the big pipe can’t happen.) The sum is \(\tfrac19 + 1 = \tfrac{10}{9}.\) Thus, C is the correct answer.
hints: For two circles of radii \(R\) and \(r\) resting on a line and touching each other, their floor contact points are \(2\sqrt{Rr}\) apart
The new pipe’s contact point is \(2\sqrt{r}\) from the big pipe’s and \(\sqrt{r}\) from the small pipe’s; it can sit between them or outside
